headline: The daughter of a jailed president leads Peru

sources.title: Keiko Fujimori sworn in as Peru president after narrow election win
Keiko Fujimori takes office as Peru's president, vowing to end decade of instability
Keiko Fujimori sworn in as Peru president after narrow election win (video, Al Jazeera English)

chunks.text: Keiko Fujimori became president of Peru on July 28, [[at the age of]] 51 and at her fourth [[attempt]]. She had lost three earlier elections. She won this one by [[fewer than]] 50,000 votes in a [[second round]] in June. She now {{takes over}} a country that has {{gone through}} eight presidents in ten years, in a system where governments rarely {{last out}} a full [[term]].

verbs.correct: To become the person in charge
To experience many things in turn
verbs.wrong: To keep the same leader for years
To be removed before the end

chunks.text: Her [[surname]] is the reason many Peruvians voted for her and the reason many others voted against. Her father, Alberto Fujimori, ruled Peru in the 1990s. During those years the state {{put down}} a violent [[rebellion]] and the economy became [[stable]]. Those same years ended with him leaving office in [[disgrace]], and he was later [[sentenced]] to 16 years in prison for [[corruption]] and for [[crimes against humanity]]. [[Supporters]] say he {{brought back}} order to a country [[close to]] [[collapse]]. [[Opponents]] say he {{did away with}} democratic limits and that people died because of it. Both of those things are [[in the record]].

verbs.correct: To stop a revolt by force

verbs.wrong: To promise something in a speech
To ignore a rule but keep it

chunks.text: Keiko Fujimori has {{taken up}} crime as her main issue. It is the topic that worries most Peruvians, according to [[pollsters]]. She has promised what she calls [[an iron fist]]. That means a very large new prison, more police on the streets, and judges whose names are not published so that criminals cannot [[threaten]] them. Human rights groups have already {{spoken out}} about those [[anonymous]] judges. Their argument is that a [[defendant]] cannot [[properly]] {{stand up for}} himself in a court when he does not know who is judging him.

verbs.wrong: To choose a new political party
To be asked to give an opinion

chunks.text: Whether she can {{hold on to}} power [[long enough to]] do any of it is the open question. Peru's [[Congress]] has {{pushed out}} several recent presidents, and her party does not control it. She has {{called on}} other parties to work [[alongside]] her. In a country that has changed leader almost every year, simply reaching the end of a full term would be unusual.

mainIdea.s: Peru swore in a new president on July 28, the daughter of a former, jailed president. She now plans a strict crime policy with judges whose names will be kept secret from the public.
mainIdea.why: The new president is the daughter of a former president who was jailed for corruption and crimes against humanity. She took office at her fourth attempt after winning by fewer than 50,000 votes in June.

mainIdea.s: A former president's daughter won Peru's presidency by a wide margin in the June election. Her party now firmly controls Congress, so lawmakers are expected to support her easily.
mainIdea.why: Close, but she won by fewer than 50,000 votes, not by a wide margin. Her party also does not control Congress, so she cannot count on easy support there.

mainIdea.s: Peru's Congress separately voted this month to lower the minimum voting age to sixteen years old. The change will take effect before the next round of regional elections across the country.
mainIdea.why: This is about a Congress vote to lower the voting age, not the new president or her crime plan.
